results.summary: This Wokwi design implements a small collection of combinational logic blocks: a NOT gate, an AND gate, a second NOT gate, and a half adder. The inputs are mapped to the gates and the outputs expose the inverted, ANDed, sum, and carry results. It is tested by toggling the input switches in the Wokwi simulator and observing the output pins. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any silicon implementation or external hardware beyond the simulator.

The design is a 2-bit multiplier that intentionally violates timing constraints to demonstrate metastable behavior in logic gates. It takes four inputs (A0, A1, B0, B1) and produces four outputs, with the internal gates sometimes outputting both 1 and 0 simultaneously before resolving. Testing involves setting all inputs to 0 then to 1 and observing the metastable outputs on LEDs. External hardware includes four switches for inputs, an external clock and reset, and four LEDs for outputs.

This project is described as a tiny time-to-digital converter (TDC) built from standard cells, though the documentation focuses on MOSFET theory and a digital watch analogy. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, and toggling the inputs causes corresponding LEDs to light up. The design is tested by switching inputs on and off to observe the LED reactions. The documentation is unclear and contains inaccuracies, making it difficult to determine the actual function.

This Wokwi design implements four basic logic gates: an inverter, an AND gate, an OR gate, and an XOR gate. It has seven input pins and four output pins, with the gates presumably connected to specific inputs. Testing is done by applying signals to the input pins and observing the outputs on the corresponding output pins. The documentation is very brief and does not specify the exact input-output mapping or any external hardware requirements.

This design uses logic gates to control segments of a 7-segment display based on input values. It has eight inputs and three outputs, which likely drive specific segments. Testing involves toggling the input switches in various combinations to see what can be displayed on the number display. No external hardware is required beyond the display itself.

This circuit uses AND and NOT logic gates to implement a simple password checker that turns on a light when the correct combination is entered. It has four input pins labeled OR and no output pins listed, though the description implies an output to control a light. Testing is done by setting the input levers to the sequence 3145. No external hardware is mentioned.

This design uses inverters, XOR, and OR gates to drive six segments of a 7-segment display, producing the letters D or O depending on the input combination. It has eight inputs and six outputs, each controlling a specific segment. Testing involves toggling switches to light up segments according to the described mapping. An external LED display is required to see the output.

This project uses inverters, including a flip-flop inverter, to light up segments of an 8-segment clock display. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, with each switch controlling a corresponding segment, and switches 3 and 4 alternating due to stored energy in the flip-flop. Testing is done by flipping switches to light up segments. An external LED display is required.

This design displays the designer's initials on a seven-segment display using logic gates. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, though the exact mapping is not detailed. Testing involves toggling switches to troubleshoot and display the initials. External hardware includes a seven-segment display and AND/OR gates.

The project aims to display a secret initial (the letter F) when a specific combination of inputs is applied. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, but the implementation is still to be decided. Testing instructions are not yet provided. The documentation is incomplete, so the actual functionality cannot be determined.
